summary:
Zénite is an interactive digital archive that tells the stories of human-made space exploration equipment left behind on the Moon, Mars, and in deep space.

Through a 3D archive, visitors can explore 12 space relics, discover their mission histories, examine NASA-sourced imagery, and learn what happened to each piece of equipment after its mission.

By preserving these stories in an accessible digital experience, Zénite gives a second life to forgotten chapters of space exploration.
details:
Zénite is an interactive digital archive designed to preserve and bring attention to the stories of human-made space exploration equipment left behind on the Moon, Mars, and in deep space. Inspired by the challenge theme "Abandoned, but Not Forgotten", the project transforms historical mission information into an engaging digital experience, helping people understand that these abandoned machines are not merely obsolete objects, but important parts of humanity's journey into space.

How it works

The platform features an interactive 3D archive containing 12 space relics. Visitors can explore the collection, browse individual records, and discover the history, purpose, achievements, and final status of each object. Each record provides historical information, technical facts, and relevant imagery, with narrated content to make exploration more engaging.

The experience also includes quizzes and exploration progress features, encouraging visitors to interact with the information rather than simply read it. The platform includes Zénite Bot, a conversational assistant designed to help users explore information about the relics and answer questions related to the archive.

The collection includes equipment from the Apollo missions, Surveyor 3, Mars Pathfinder, Spirit and Opportunity, Viking 1, Pioneer 10 and 11, Ingenuity, and Voyager 1 and 2.

Benefits and intended impact

Zénite makes historical information about space exploration equipment more accessible, engaging, and easier to discover. It helps visitors understand the scientific and historical importance of machines that remain on other celestial bodies or continue travelling through space.

Our intended impact is educational and cultural: to encourage curiosity about space exploration, raise awareness of the legacy of past missions, and preserve the stories behind equipment that is often overlooked after its mission ends. We want people to recognize that even when a mission is over, its contributions to science and exploration remain valuable.

Technologies and tools used

Zénite was developed using modern web technologies. The main tools and technologies include:

  • Nuxt 4 and Vue 3: application structure and user interface.
  • Three.js: interactive 3D archive experience.
  • GSAP: interface animations and visual transitions.
  • Lenis: smooth scrolling experience.
  • Tailwind CSS 4: interface styling.
  • Supabase: PostgreSQL database, authentication, and file storage.
  • Vercel: application deployment and hosting.
  • Microsoft Edge Text-to-Speech: generation of synthetic narration from original project texts.
  • Vitest, ESLint, and Vue TypeScript tools: testing, code quality, and type checking.

The project also uses NASA's Image and Video Library and official NASA mission resources as references for its historical information and imagery. The current archive contains 24 images with corresponding source references and credits. No specialized hardware was required; development was carried out using standard computer-based software tools.

Creative approach

The central creative idea behind Zénite is to transform an archive into an experience of exploration. Instead of presenting abandoned space equipment through a conventional list of articles, we created an interactive 3D environment where each relic becomes an entry point into a larger story about human exploration.

The combination of 3D visualization, historical records, narration, quizzes, and a conversational assistant brings together educational content and interactive storytelling. The project gives visibility to objects that are physically distant, often forgotten, and rarely discussed outside specialized space-related contexts.

Factors considered by the team

During development, the team considered historical accuracy, the reliability of information sources, proper attribution of NASA imagery, and the distinction between photographs, illustrations, artistic concepts, and scale models. We also considered usability, accessibility of information, the clarity of the interface, and the importance of making the experience engaging for people with different levels of knowledge about space exploration.

Ultimately, Zénite was built around one central idea: a machine does not have to be active to remain meaningful. Its mission may have ended, but its story, discoveries, and contribution to humanity should not be forgotten.
